options.content: A rigid member carrying loads across a span between supports
A rope or cable that carries a pulling force only
options.rationale: That is a cable or tie.

options.content: A vertical column that carries a roof down to the ground
options.rationale: That is a column or pillar.

options.content: A riveted joint that holds two steel plates together

explanation: A beam is a long rigid member, usually horizontal, carrying loads across a span.

stem: A plank resting on two bricks has a heavy load placed at its centre. Which part of the plank is in tension?

options.rationale: Correct: it is stretched as the plank sags.
That is the neutral axis: no stress.

options.content: The ends resting on the bricks
options.rationale: The bending stresses are greatest in the middle of the span.

explanation: As the plank sags, the bottom is stretched (tension) and the top squashed (compression).

stem: What name is given to the layer in a bending beam that is neither stretched nor squashed?
explanation: The neutral axis (neutral zone) carries no tension or compression.

stem: A wooden plank is to be used as a beam. How should it be placed to sag least under a load?

options.content: Flat, so its greater dimension is horizontal
On its edge, so its greater dimension is vertical

options.rationale: Then it is no longer a beam across a span.

explanation: A deeper beam puts its top and bottom surfaces further from the neutral axis, making it much stiffer and stronger.

stem: Why are steel roof beams often made with an I-shaped cross-section?

options.content: I-sections are the cheapest and quickest shape to make.
options.rationale: Cost is not the main reason.

options.content: The thin web in the middle carries most of the bending load.
options.rationale: The flanges carry most of the bending stress.

options.content: Most material sits in the flanges, where the stress is greatest.
I-sections never bend, however large the load on them.

explanation: Material near the neutral axis does little work; the I-section moves it to the flanges, far from the axis, where it is most effective.
hints: Where in a bending beam are the stresses largest?

stem: Why are steel rods placed near the bottom of a reinforced concrete beam supported at both ends?

options.content: The bottom is in compression and steel is weak in compression.
The bottom is in tension, and concrete is weak in tension while steel is strong.

explanation: Concrete resists compression well but cracks under tension; the steel takes the tension in the stretched lower part.
hints: Which part of the beam is stretched?

stem: Match each effect with its description.

right.content: Layers of material slide over each other
A long thin member bends sideways when compressed

explanation: These are the four ways forces act inside structural members.

stem: Material near the neutral axis of a beam carries little stress, so hollow beams can be almost as strong as solid ones for much less mass.
explanation: Removing material from near the neutral axis (box sections, tubes) saves weight with little loss of strength.

stem: Learners fold strips of card of the same size into beams of different cross-sections: flat, L-section and box section. Each is supported at its ends and the same load is hung from its centre.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which beam is likely to sag most?

options.rationale: It is deeper than the flat strip.
Correct: it has the smallest depth.
Same material, different shapes, different stiffness.

parts.explanation: The flat strip has almost no depth, so it is the least stiff.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why this is a fair test of the effect of cross-sectional shape.

points.description: The same amount of the same material (same mass per unit length) is used for every beam
The span, the position of the load and its size are kept the same, so only the shape changes

explanation: Only the cross-section changes; the shapes with more depth (box, L) are stiffer than the flat strip.
hints: What must be kept the same in a fair test?

stem: Which of these is a hollow beam section?
explanation: A box section is a hollow rectangular tube.

stem: A thin steel rod is used to support a heavy load by pushing up on it from below. What failure is most likely if the rod is long and thin?

options.rationale: The rod is compressed, not stretched.
Not the main risk for a column.
Not a structural failure under load.
Correct: long thin members under compression bend sideways.

explanation: Under compression, a long thin member is liable to buckle: bend sideways and collapse well before the material itself is crushed.
hints: Is the rod being pushed or pulled?
